---
title: "Cluster-Randomized and Factorial Experiments"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
```

The cookbooks and the other articles all randomize individual subjects to one of two
arms. This article covers the two other treatment structures EDI has designs for:

1. **Cluster-randomized experiments.** Whole groups (schools, clinics, villages,
   households) are randomized, and outcomes are measured on the individuals inside
   them. The designs are `DesignFixedCluster` and `DesignFixedBlockedCluster`.
2. **Factorial experiments.** Subjects get a combination of levels of several
   treatment factors. The design is `DesignFixedFactorial`. Its current support is
   limited to two arms, and the section below says exactly what it can and cannot
   do, and how to run and analyze a 2 x 2 factorial with the pieces EDI has today.

It assumes you know the four steps of an EDI analysis (design, assign, record
responses, infer) from [Get started](EDI.html) or the
[continuous cookbook](cookbook-continuous.html).

# Part 1: cluster-randomized experiments

## Why the cluster changes the analysis

When a school is randomized, every student in it gets the same arm, and students in
the same school also share teachers, neighborhoods and test conditions. Their outcomes
are correlated. The information about the treatment effect then grows with the number
of *schools*, not the number of students. An analysis that treats the students as
independently randomized overstates the sample size, so its standard errors are too
small and its p-values too small. The section
[What goes wrong if you ignore the clusters](#what-goes-wrong-if-you-ignore-the-clusters)
shows how badly.

## A school trial

Thirty-two schools take part, with 15 to 25 students each. Half the schools are
randomized to a new curriculum. Each student has a pretest score; the outcome is an
end-of-year test score. Schools differ from each other (a school effect with standard
deviation 4 points) on top of student-level noise (standard deviation 6 points). The
true effect of the curriculum is 3 points.

```{r school-data}
set.seed(20261117)
G = 32
school_size = sample(15:25, G, replace = TRUE)
school = factor(rep(sprintf("S%02d", 1:G), times = school_size))
n = length(school)
X = data.frame(school = school, pretest = round(rnorm(n, 50, 10)))
n
```

### The design: name the cluster column

`DesignFixedCluster` takes the name of the column of `X` that identifies each
subject's cluster as `cluster_col`. The cluster column stays in `X`, but it is an
assignment label, not a covariate: it is left out of the default `~ .` covariate
model that the regression-based inference classes fit.

```{r cluster-design}
des = DesignFixedCluster$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", cluster_col = "school",
                             verbose = FALSE)
des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
w = des$get_w()
```

`w` is the usual 0/1 vector with one entry per student. Every student in a school has
the same value, and `prob_T = 0.5` (the default) means half the *schools* are treated.
Because the schools have different sizes, the share of *students* treated is not
exactly one half.

```{r cluster-check}
all(tapply(w, school, function(s) length(unique(s))) == 1)   # one arm per school
table(w_school = tapply(w, school, max))
mean(w)
```

Every redraw from the design has the same structure. This is what the randomization
test uses as its reference distribution:

```{r cluster-redraws}
draws = des$draw_ws_according_to_design(1000)
all(apply(draws, 2, function(v) all(tapply(v, school, function(s) length(unique(s))) == 1)))
table(colSums(draws[!duplicated(school), ]))   # treated schools per redraw
```

Now record the outcomes.

```{r cluster-outcomes}
true_effect = 3
school_effect = rnorm(G, sd = 4)[as.integer(school)]
y = 60 + true_effect * w + 0.5 * (X$pretest - 50) + school_effect + rnorm(n, sd = 6)
des$add_all_subject_responses(y)
```

### Which inference respects the clustering

On a cluster design, EDI's procedures fall into two groups.

**Cluster-aware on every inference class that offers them:**

* **Randomization test and interval** (`compute_rand_two_sided_pval()`,
  `compute_rand_confidence_interval()`). The reference distribution is built from
  `draw_ws_according_to_design()`, so it re-randomizes whole schools, exactly as the
  trial did. A few classes do not offer a randomization interval (for example
  `InferenceSurvivalRestrictedMeanDiff` and the log-rank tests); check
  `inf$supports("randomization_ci")`.
* **Nonparametric bootstrap** (`compute_bootstrap_confidence_interval()`,
  `compute_bootstrap_two_sided_pval()`). The design resamples whole schools with
  replacement, not students. A cluster bootstrap behaves like an asymptotic method
  whose sample size is the number of clusters, not subjects, so it needs enough
  clusters. With fewer than about 30 clusters its intervals tend to be too narrow and
  its tests reject too often; with 10 clusters, an RMST percentile interval rejected
  a true null about 11 to 13% of the time at a nominal 5%. With few clusters prefer
  the randomization test.
* **Jackknife** (`compute_jackknife_wald_confidence_interval()`,
  `compute_jackknife_wald_two_sided_pval()`, `compute_jackknife_std_error()`). On a
  cluster design the default `unit = "auto"` drops one cluster at a time; you can
  also say `unit = "cluster"` explicitly.

**Wald (asymptotic) inference depends on the class:**

* `InferenceContinOLS` and `InferenceContinLin` switch to a CR2 (Bell-McCaffrey)
  cluster-robust standard error with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (`G - 1` if
  those cannot be computed) when the design is a cluster design.
* Every other class still computes its Wald, score, likelihood-ratio and
  parametric-bootstrap results as if subjects were independent. It says so with a
  warning of class `edi_cluster_independence_warning`, once per object and procedure
  family. Treat that warning as "use the randomization test, bootstrap or jackknife
  instead". OLS and Lin also give this warning for their likelihood-based procedures,
  which have no cluster-robust version.

EDI has no mixed-model (random cluster effect) analysis for cluster designs. Its
GLMM classes (such as `InferenceContinKKGLMM`) model matched pairs from the KK
matching designs, not clusters.

### Running the analysis

`InferenceContinOLS` regresses the outcome on treatment and `pretest`. Its Wald
interval and p-value use the CR2 cluster-robust standard error:

```{r cluster-ols}
inf = InferenceContinOLS$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
inf$num_cores = 1L

est = inf$compute_estimate()
ci_wald = inf$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
est; ci_wald
inf$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
```

The estimate is `r round(est, 2)` points against a true effect of `r true_effect`.
With only 32 schools, an error of this size is not surprising: the interval is wide
because the school effects add noise that does not average away over students.

The randomization test and its inverted interval re-randomize whole schools. Setting
the argument `r` (the number of redraws) to 500 keeps this page fast; use more in a real analysis.

```{r cluster-rand}
inf$set_seed(1)
inf$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE)
inf$set_seed(1)
inf$compute_rand_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05, r = 500, show_progress = FALSE)
```

The cluster bootstrap resamples schools. The percentile interval is used here; a BCa
interval also works but needs `B` of about 501 or more.

```{r cluster-boot}
inf$set_seed(1)
inf$compute_bootstrap_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05, B = 501, type = "percentile",
                                          show_progress = FALSE)
```

The delete-one-school jackknife:

```{r cluster-jack}
inf$compute_jackknife_std_error(unit = "cluster")
inf$compute_jackknife_wald_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05, unit = "cluster")
```

All four agree roughly, and all are about as wide as you would expect from 32
schools.

A class without a cluster-robust Wald variance warns. The simple difference in means
is the example here; its randomization test is still cluster-aware and gives no
warning.

```{r cluster-warning, strict_expect_warning = TRUE}
inf_diff = InferenceAllSimpleAverageDiff$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
inf_diff$num_cores = 1L
inf_diff$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()      # warns: SE treats students as independent
inf_diff$set_seed(1)
inf_diff$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE)   # no warning
```

If you have read the warning and only want the cluster-aware procedures to print, wrap
the call in `suppressWarnings(expr, classes = "edi_cluster_independence_warning")`.

## What goes wrong if you ignore the clusters

Suppose the same data were analyzed as if each student had been randomized on their
own. That is what you get by declaring an individual-level design (here
`DesignFixedBernoulli`) and supplying the observed assignment, as in
[Analyzing an existing experiment](analyzing-an-existing-experiment.html):

```{r naive-design}
des_naive = DesignFixedBernoulli$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
des_naive$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X[, "pretest", drop = FALSE])
des_naive$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = w)
des_naive$add_all_subject_responses(y)

inf_naive = InferenceContinOLS$new(des_naive, verbose = FALSE)
inf_naive$num_cores = 1L
inf_naive$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
inf_naive$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
inf_naive$set_seed(1)
inf_naive$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE)
```

The point estimate is the same, but the interval is much narrower and both p-values
are much smaller. The naive randomization test is wrong too: it re-randomizes
individual students, which is not how the trial was run. EDI cannot catch this
mistake for you, since nothing in the data says the treatment was assigned by school.
Declaring the design that matches the real assignment is the analyst's job.

### A small simulation

How much too narrow? The simulation below repeats the trial 200 times with a smaller
setup (20 schools of 20 students, school-effect standard deviation 0.5, student-level
standard deviation 1, so the intraclass correlation is 0.2) and records whether each
95% Wald interval covers the true effect. It is small so that the page builds quickly;
the Monte Carlo standard error of each coverage figure is about 1.5 percentage points
near 95%.

```{r sim}
sim_once = function(G = 20, m = 20, beta = 0.5, sd_school = 0.5, sd_student = 1) {
  school = factor(rep(seq_len(G), each = m))
  n = G * m
  X = data.frame(school = school, x = rnorm(n))

  d = DesignFixedCluster$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", cluster_col = "school",
                             verbose = FALSE)
  d$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
  d$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
  w = d$get_w()
  y = beta * w + X$x + rnorm(G, sd = sd_school)[school] + rnorm(n, sd = sd_student)
  d$add_all_subject_responses(y)

  d0 = DesignFixedBernoulli$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
  d0$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X[, "x", drop = FALSE])
  d0$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = w)
  d0$add_all_subject_responses(y)

  ci_cluster = InferenceContinOLS$new(d, verbose = FALSE)$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
  ci_naive = InferenceContinOLS$new(d0, verbose = FALSE)$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
  c(cover_cluster = unname(ci_cluster[1] <= beta & beta <= ci_cluster[2]),
    cover_naive   = unname(ci_naive[1] <= beta & beta <= ci_naive[2]),
    width_cluster = unname(diff(ci_cluster)),
    width_naive   = unname(diff(ci_naive)))
}

set.seed(1)
res = t(replicate(200, sim_once()))
round(colMeans(res), 3)
```

The cluster-robust interval covers close to its nominal 95%. The naive interval is
less than half as wide and misses the true effect far more often than 5% of the time.
The gap grows with cluster size and with the intraclass correlation: the variance
inflation from clustering (the "design effect") is roughly $1 + (m - 1)\rho$ for
clusters of size $m$ and intraclass correlation $\rho$, which is
$1 + 19 \times 0.2 = 4.8$ here.

## Blocking the clusters: `DesignFixedBlockedCluster`

If clusters fall into natural strata (districts, regions, clinic types), randomizing
clusters within each stratum keeps the arms balanced on the stratum.
`DesignFixedBlockedCluster` takes both `strata_cols` and `cluster_col`. Within each
block, `prob_T` of the clusters are treated, and each cluster must lie within a single
block (the design errors otherwise).

Here 32 schools sit in four districts, eight per district. Blocks and clusters need
not have the same number of subjects: the unit randomized is the cluster, so each
block simply treats `prob_T` of its own clusters (rounded at random when that is not a
whole number), whatever the school and district sizes. This example gives every
school 20 students only to keep the simulation simple.

```{r blocked-cluster}
set.seed(20261118)
G = 32
school = factor(rep(sprintf("S%02d", 1:G), each = 20))
district = factor(rep(rep(c("North", "South", "East", "West"), each = 8), each = 20))
n = length(school)
Xb = data.frame(school = school, district = district, pretest = round(rnorm(n, 50, 10)))

des_b = DesignFixedBlockedCluster$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous",
                                      strata_cols = "district", cluster_col = "school",
                                      verbose = FALSE)
des_b$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(Xb)
des_b$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
wb = des_b$get_w()
table(district = district[!duplicated(school)], treated = tapply(wb, school, unique))
```

Each district has four treated and four control schools. The district column is
also a covariate (it is in `X` and is not the cluster column), so OLS adjusts for it.
The randomization test re-randomizes schools within districts, and the bootstrap
resamples schools within districts.

```{r blocked-cluster-inference}
yb = 60 + 3 * wb + 0.5 * (Xb$pretest - 50) + rnorm(G, sd = 4)[as.integer(school)] +
  rnorm(n, sd = 6)
des_b$add_all_subject_responses(yb)

inf_b = InferenceContinOLS$new(des_b, verbose = FALSE)
inf_b$num_cores = 1L
inf_b$compute_estimate()
inf_b$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
inf_b$set_seed(1)
inf_b$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE)
inf_b$set_seed(1)
inf_b$compute_bootstrap_confidence_interval(B = 501, type = "percentile",
                                            show_progress = FALSE)
```

The cluster jackknife is not available on this design: on a blocked design,
`compute_jackknife_wald_confidence_interval()` returns `NA` with a warning for
`unit = "auto"`, `"cluster"` and `"observation"`. `unit = "block"` drops a whole
district at a time, and with four districts that is too few deletion units: EDI
returns `NA` with a warning for any jackknife with fewer than five. Use the
randomization test or the bootstrap.

## Checklist for cluster trials

* Put the cluster ID in `X` and name it as `cluster_col`. Make it a factor or
  character column with no missing values.
* Use the randomization test, the bootstrap or the cluster jackknife with any
  inference class. For a Wald interval, use `InferenceContinOLS` or
  `InferenceContinLin`, which are cluster-robust on these designs.
* Heed `edi_cluster_independence_warning`: the procedure it names treats subjects as
  independent.
* Do not put the cluster column in a custom `model_formula`. Treatment is constant
  within clusters, so cluster indicators are collinear with it; EDI warns
  (`edi_cluster_col_in_model_formula_warning`).
* Plan the number of clusters, not just the number of subjects. With few clusters
  (say, under 20) every procedure has limited precision, and the randomization test,
  which is exact for the sharp null, is the safest choice. Use the cluster bootstrap
  only with about 30 or more clusters; below that it is anti-conservative.
* If an existing cluster trial was randomized by someone else, declare
  `DesignFixedCluster` (or `DesignFixedBlockedCluster`) and pass the recorded
  assignment with `assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = )`. Then check that
  `w` is constant within clusters.

# Part 2: factorial experiments

## What `DesignFixedFactorial` supports today

A factorial experiment crosses two or more treatment factors: in a 2 x 2 factorial,
factor A (say, a text reminder) and factor B (say, a small incentive) are each on or
off, giving four cells. Each subject gets one cell.

`DesignFixedFactorial` takes the factors as a named list of their numbers of levels.
**At present the product of the levels must be exactly 2**, so the only accepted
input is a single two-level factor such as `list(reminder = 2)`. A true 2 x 2
(`list(A = 2, B = 2)`) or a three-level factor errors in the constructor:

```{r factorial-2x2-error}
tryCatch(
  DesignFixedFactorial$new(n = 40, response_type = "continuous",
                           factors = list(reminder = 2, incentive = 2)),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
```

Support for more than two cells is planned along with EDI's multi-arm designs. Until
then:

* With a single two-level factor, `DesignFixedFactorial` is a balanced complete
  randomization: exactly half of the subjects (off by at most one when `n` is odd)
  are in each arm. It works with every inference class, like any other two-arm design.
* EDI has no main-effect or interaction estimates for multi-factor designs. A 2 x 2
  can still be run and its main effects analyzed with EDI's blocked designs; the
  interaction needs a regression outside EDI. Both are shown below.

## A one-factor `DesignFixedFactorial`

`w` is coded {0, 1} (1 = treated) both internally and in the public accessors, the
same as every other EDI design. `get_w_factorial()` returns the factor levels as a
data frame with one column per factor, using levels `1:levels`. For a two-level
factor, `w = 0` is level 1 and `w = 1` is level 2.

```{r factorial-one}
set.seed(20261119)
n = 40
Xf = data.frame(age = round(rnorm(n, 40, 10)))

des_f = DesignFixedFactorial$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous",
                                 factors = list(reminder = 2), verbose = FALSE)
des_f$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(Xf)
des_f$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
w_f = des_f$get_w()
table(w_f)
head(data.frame(w = w_f, des_f$get_w_factorial(), row.names = NULL))
```

From here the analysis is the same as for any two-arm design:

```{r factorial-one-inference}
y_f = 10 + 2 * w_f + 0.1 * Xf$age + rnorm(n, sd = 2)
des_f$add_all_subject_responses(y_f)

inf_f = InferenceContinOLS$new(des_f, verbose = FALSE)
inf_f$num_cores = 1L
inf_f$compute_estimate()
inf_f$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
inf_f$set_seed(1)
inf_f$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE)
```

The randomization test redraws balanced allocations, as the design did. The
nonparametric bootstrap resamples subjects without keeping the arms exactly
balanced, which makes it slightly conservative on this design.

## Running a 2 x 2 factorial with blocked designs

A balanced 2 x 2 with `n` subjects puts `n / 4` in each cell. The same assignment
can be produced in two steps: randomize factor A with equal arms, then randomize
factor B with equal arms *within each level of A*. The second step is a blocked
design with A as the stratum. Seen from either factor, the result is a balanced
randomization blocked on the other factor, and that is what the analysis declares.

Eighty participants; A is a reminder, B an incentive. The outcome is a continuous
engagement score.

```{r ff-assign}
set.seed(20261120)
n = 80
Xff = data.frame(age = round(rnorm(n, 40, 10)))

# Step 1: factor A, balanced
des_A = DesignFixedFactorial$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous",
                                 factors = list(reminder = 2), verbose = FALSE)
des_A$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(Xff)
des_A$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
A = des_A$get_w()

# Step 2: factor B, balanced within each level of A
des_B = DesignFixedBlocking$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", strata_cols = "A",
                                verbose = FALSE)
des_B$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(data.frame(Xff, A = factor(A)))
des_B$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
B = des_B$get_w()

table(A, B)
```

Every cell has 20 participants. The outcomes below have a reminder effect of 2 when
there is no incentive and 3 when there is one, an incentive effect of 1 without the
reminder and 2 with it: an interaction of 1. The main effect of each factor (its
effect averaged over the two levels of the other factor) is therefore 2.5 for the
reminder and 1.5 for the incentive.

```{r ff-outcomes}
y_ff = 20 + 2 * A + 1 * B + 1 * A * B + 0.1 * (Xff$age - 40) + rnorm(n, sd = 2)
```

### Main effects

To analyze the main effect of A, declare the design that describes how A was
assigned *given B*: a balanced randomization of A within each level of B. That is
`DesignFixedBlocking` with `strata_cols = "B"`, with the observed A supplied as
`w_precomputed`. B is in `X`, so OLS adjusts for it; in a balanced 2 x 2, the
coefficient on A in a model with A and B (and no interaction) is the average of A's
effect at the two levels of B, which is the main effect. The randomization test
permutes A within the levels of B, which keeps every cell at 20, as in the real
assignment.

```{r ff-main-A}
X_for_A = data.frame(Xff, B = factor(B))
des_mA = DesignFixedBlocking$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", strata_cols = "B",
                                 verbose = FALSE)
des_mA$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X_for_A)
des_mA$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = A)
des_mA$add_all_subject_responses(y_ff)

inf_A = InferenceContinOLS$new(des_mA, verbose = FALSE)
inf_A$num_cores = 1L
inf_A$compute_estimate()
inf_A$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
inf_A$set_seed(1)
inf_A$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE)
```

The main effect of B is the same analysis with the roles swapped:

```{r ff-main-B}
X_for_B = data.frame(Xff, A = factor(A))
des_mB = DesignFixedBlocking$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", strata_cols = "A",
                                 verbose = FALSE)
des_mB$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X_for_B)
des_mB$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = B)
des_mB$add_all_subject_responses(y_ff)

inf_B = InferenceContinOLS$new(des_mB, verbose = FALSE)
inf_B$num_cores = 1L
inf_B$compute_estimate()
inf_B$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
inf_B$set_seed(1)
inf_B$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE)
```

Each estimate should be read as "the effect of this factor, averaged over the two
levels of the other". When the interaction is large, the average can hide effects of
different sizes (or even opposite signs) in the two levels, so look at the
interaction before reporting main effects alone.

### The interaction

No EDI class estimates the A x B interaction. It is the difference between A's effect
when B = 1 and A's effect when B = 0, which is the coefficient on `A:B` in an
ordinary regression with both factors and their product. Base R's `lm()` gives it
with a model-based standard error:

```{r ff-interaction}
fit = lm(y_ff ~ A * B + age, data = data.frame(y_ff, A, B, age = Xff$age))
round(summary(fit)$coefficients["A:B", ], 3)
round(confint(fit)["A:B", ], 3)
```

Note how the coefficients of this model differ from main effects. With the product
term in the model, the coefficient on `A` is A's effect *when B = 0* (a simple
effect), not its main effect. Main effects come from the EDI analyses above (or, in
`lm()`, from a model without the product term, or with A and B coded -1/+1).

A 2 x 2 factorial is usually sized to estimate main effects. An interaction of the
same size is estimated with twice the standard error, so a trial powered for main
effects has little power for the interaction. A non-significant interaction test here
is weak evidence that there is no interaction.

### What this recipe does not cover

* Unequal cells. The recipe assumes `n` divisible by 4 and equal cells. With other
  allocations, the per-factor blocked designs no longer reproduce the joint
  assignment exactly; check `draw_ws_according_to_design()` against the real cell
  counts before trusting a randomization test.
* More than two levels per factor, or more than two factors.
* A randomization test of the interaction. Testing "no interaction" does not fix all
  potential outcomes under the null, so a simple permutation test does not apply.
